summary: Nine waves, A to I, each one plan of about 16 to 25 hours, placing all 36 planned cards. A to C stay what Tony has seen (mail; the web, photos and PDFs; typed facts, notes, calendar questions, the 21:00 text and reminders), with each risky part switched on only after its own check. From D on each wave adds at most one new kind of risk, behind the gate that kind needs and lowest first: quiet no-model watchers (D), pages and logs both parents share (E), harder reading with a read-only browser and voice memos (F, no new kind), ways to send out (G), acting in the house (H), and last a paired phone and the screen-control pilot (I, two kinds because the pilot is itself a paired device). Everything Happy can read is in place before the first tool that sends outside the one-to-one chat exists, so the recipient test in wave G runs once against all of it, and nothing touches the house or a device until the rest has run for weeks.

plan_size.basis: M0 was 50 steps and M1 was 49 steps in nine phases whose own estimates add up to about 20 hours, written for 8 to 10 hours a week, so one plan is two to three weeks of work with one exit gate of about 3 hours; every figure below is an estimate built from the card hours in the sizing file plus about 0.75 hours to get ready and 3 hours for the exit gate, with steps counted at M1's rate of a little under half an hour a step.

notes: Size, all estimates: about 180 hours and about 360 steps across the nine waves (146.5 card hours from the sizing file plus about 3.75 hours of getting ready and exit gate per wave), which is roughly 18 to 23 weeks at 8 to 10 hours a week, plus the fixed waits. Nothing here has been tried on the Mac.

Why nine and not fewer: 146.5 card hours could be packed into seven plans only with every wave at its ceiling and the kinds of risk mixed. Nine keeps each wave from D on to one kind of risk with its gate inside it, and leaves room in each wave from B on for the piece that gives way from the wave before: with that piece carried, B is about 23.5 hours, D at most 20.25, E 23.25, F 23.25, G 22.75, H 20.5 and I 23.75.

What changed in A to C against what Tony has seen, and why. Wave A now holds both inboxes and the lookup and is at its ceiling (25 hours), so the two paper cards (the stop-and-check sheet with T8, and Jordan's half page; 1.5 hours) moved to wave B; they add no risk and gate nothing in A. The device deny list left wave B for wave I, where the first device is paired (S14). The day out moved from C to D because C is full with every answer yes. 'Email me this' was a fill-in in C and is now in wave G with the other ways to send out. The handbook was 'next in line' for C and is in wave E.

Mail runs on one layer from wave A until wave C's plugin phase: tool permissions, an explicit deny and two tests, without the roadmap's coded check on who may call the connector. That is the approved S1. T5's connector turn in wave C decides whether that rule can be written at all; if it cannot, Tony decides then whether one layer is enough for the calendar too.

The riskiest combination in A to C appears at the end of wave B: a parent's own agent then holds private chat and mail answers, reads photos and PDFs directly, and can hand a task to a helper that fetches any public address. Only a prompt rule and planted tests stand between them; the roadmap calls that hand-off its one remaining leak path. Tony signs it in wave B's exit gate. The harder line, if he ever wants it, is to switch the lookup off.

Order of F and G. I put harder reading (F) before ways to send out (G) because it adds no new kind of risk and because the roadmap's test 'an injected web page cannot change the email recipient' is then run once, with the browser already present. The shared list and 'email me this' are probably used more than voice memos and the browser, so the two waves can swap: neither needs the other, and the cost is re-running the injected-page recipient test when the browser arrives. D and E can swap the same way.

Wave I, one thing to know: the deny list is Gateway-wide, so lifting the two entries for the screen-control pilot lifts them for Tony's paired phone too. The card's own step is to re-read the phone's approved command list first; if that shows a command the lift would open on the phone, Tony decides at that point, for example by revoking the phone for the length of the pilot with the command already on the printed sheet. Until wave I nothing in config covers a device paired by mistake; the written rule is no Mac app, no pairing and no setup code, and the one documented line against screen control can ride along in any earlier deploy if he wants a visible 'no' sooner.

Tests that can end or shrink a card, each placed where its answer is first needed: T1 (day 8, wave A: a weekly sign-in or a different connector); T4 (waves A, B and H: the only documented fix changes a signed-off setting); T5 (waves C, F and G: a rule that cannot see its fields cannot be written); T6 (wave C: the fallback reverses two signed-off settings and needs Tony's yes); T7 (wave C: if a reminder cannot be created from iMessage, reminders, flyer dates and project check-ins are not built and Tony decides what comes next); T9 (wave G: the shared-list card is dropped and recipe ingredients come back as text); the browser image build (wave F); step zero (wave I). T2 is in A and C, T3 in A and D, T8 in B. T10 is in no wave: its only user, an envelope for Jordan, is not planned.

What works for Jordan and what does not. She gets the 07:00 mail text, the lookup, web answers, photos and PDFs, notes, calendar questions, the handbook, the grid, the dose log, voice memos, the shared list, the group chat, 'email me this', printing and lights. She is not a command owner, so timed reminders, flyer reminders and project check-ins are Tony's only, and her copies of the evening text, the conflict watch, the weekly text and the monthly coverage text are separate jobs that Tony says are switched on at execution.

Children's data. From wave C the two children's first names, school years and school district go to the cloud model with every chat of a parent's own agent. From wave E the dose log keeps what was given for 14 days and sends it to the cloud model when read back, on Tony's confirm step. Web searches and helper tasks may carry the town and ages, never names or the school, which is a prompt rule checked by a canary, not an enforced limit. The kids agent stays parked.

Roadmap lines that are not carried, each by Tony's own answer or an approved simplification: a local model for mail (cloud model with the Zero Data Retention application filed); the blocking firewall and proxy before mail (answer 7a: one rule first); the prompt-injection tripwire (answer 7c: waits for local models); the secret egress proxy (nothing for it to act on); groups disabled (re-opened for one chat in wave G); one data domain per person (the handbook, the database and busy-only calendar sharing are shared on purpose). Nothing on the never list is added in any wave, every scheduled text goes only to its owner, and no agent sends into another person's conversation.

Fixed waits that set the calendar: day 8 of the Google sign-in in A; one night of the proxy in report mode and a day between the two parents' agents in B; two-day exit tests in C and D; one evening in H.

Unverified: every hour and step figure; my splits of F020, F076, OCL-01 and MAC-02 into phases; and everything the cards themselves list as not tried, in particular the connector's flags (it is not installed), whether a blocking check sees connector, scheduling, browser and send calls, whether a command job can use a stored calendar sign-in, and whether screen control works inside a virtual Mac at all.
Missing details never hold a wave: each is listed under tony_provides for the wave that uses it. The only items that wait for something outside the plan are the two parked cards.
